title: The hypertrophy series: the issue of volume without intensity
summary: NH explains that volume and intensity can't exist apart and combine into tonnage. He argues against high-volume, low-intensity training for three reasons: it is time-inefficient for building tonnage, cardiovascular and mechanical fatigue end sets before the muscle fails, and heavy weights bring mental, progression, stretch-reflex and hormonal benefits that matter for naturals.

claims.claim: Tonnage is tonnage and any tension creates some growth, but strategy matters more as you advance, because advanced lifters need more tonnage and stimulus.
Volume and intensity can't exist without each other and together form tonnage, while frequency can stand alone.
Any set at a given percentage implies a rep count, and any set/rep scheme (e.g. 10x3) implies an intensity, because each set falls somewhere on your exhaustion range.
'Intensity training' and 'volume training' only describe a skew; both contain both notions, and in general high reps sit lower on intensity and low reps lower on volume.
Reason 1 against low-intensity, high-volume work: heavy weights accumulate tonnage much faster (e.g. squat reps at 300 lbs vs 45 lbs); sets of 100 would make workouts last four hours.
Some studies point to heavy weights being better for growth, but the main issue is the difficulty of accumulating tonnage with light weights.

Reason 2: sets of 50 reps on compounds turn into cardio and exhaust cardiovascular endurance before the muscles; posture and technique also fail mechanically, shifting work away from the target muscles.
Reason 3 (less certain): heavy weights benefit mental health and fortitude and open more progression schemes; high-rep work can end from the pump while the muscle could continue.
Light, high-rep work lacks the stretch reflex and hormonal boost of heavy compound lifts, which matter for naturals trying to slowly raise testosterone production.
Low-intensity, high-volume work can have benefits, but shouldn't be your main method; if you use it, understand why and its limits.
RPE or percentage-based programming matters for accumulating quality tonnage.
